metadata.title: Temporal associations of psychological readiness and functional outcomes with return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Psychological readiness is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of return to sport (RTS) and return to preinjury level (RTPre) of sport after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Functional outcomes are also relevant. However, the clinical significance of psychological readiness and functional outcomes may vary depending on the postoperative time point, and the association of psychological readiness and functional outcomes with RTS may be temporal. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the temporal association of psychological readiness and functional outcomes with RTS at different postoperative time points (≤6 months, <6-12 months, >12 months) after ACL reconstruction. METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42025630743), 6 databases (MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), CINAHL, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus) were searched from January 1st, 2008 to April 1st, 2026. Data on psychological measures (ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (ACL-RSI), Knee Self-Efficacy Scale (K-SES), Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK)), functional outcomes (International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) for knee flexion strength (FLEX-LSI), knee extension strength (EXT-LSI), and single-leg hop distance (SH-LSI)) were extracted from all eligible studies comparing these outcomes between RTS and non-RTS groups, as well as RTPre and non-RTPre groups following primary ACL reconstruction. Effect sizes were pooled as mean differences (continuous variable) or risk ratios (dichotomous variable). Subgroup analyses were stratified by postoperative follow-up time points: ≤6 months, >6-12 months, and >12 months. RESULTS: A total of 25 studies comprising 7174 patients were included. Overall, the RTS rate was 79.3%, whereas the RTPre rate was 44.1%. The RTPre group exhibited significantly higher ACL-RSI scores than the non-RTPre group, and intergroup difference in ACL-RSI widened progressively over time following ACL reconstruction (≤6 months: mean difference (MD) = 16.09, 95% confidence interval (95%CI): 9.13-23.05; >6-12 months: MD = 18.64, 95%CI: 14.64-22.63; >12 months: MD = 27.07, 95%CI: 22.37-31.76). Similar patterns were observed in the comparison of RTS and non-RTS groups. Compared with the non-RTS group, the RTS group showed higher K-SES scores (MD = 1.27, 95%CI: 1.06-1.87; p < 0.0001) and reduced kinesiophobia (TSK/TSK-11, standardized mean difference (SMD) = -1.15, 95%CI: -2.10 to -0.19, p = 0.02). The RTS group also demonstrated superior functional outcomes vs. the non-RTS group, including IKDC (MD = 7.52, 95%CI: 5.85-9.19), KOOS-Sport/Rec (MD = 11.32, 95%CI: 8.84-13.81), KOOS-quality of life (QoL) (MD = 13.97, 95%CI: 10.83-17.10), EXT-LSI (MD = 7.48%, 95%CI: 2.69-12.26), FLEX-LSI (MD = 3.67%, 95%CI: 0.91-6.43), SH-LSI (MD = 2.96%, 95%CI: 1.77-4.16), though IKDC differences remained below established minimal clinically important difference thresholds. CONCLUSION: Psychological readiness assessed via the ACL-RSI is important for RTS evaluation after ACL reconstruction. Our analyses uniquely reveal widening between-group gaps in psychological readiness at later recovery stages, with minimal temporal changes in functional differences. Longitudinal monitoring and serial ACL-RSI evaluation across varied postoperative phases is recommended alongside functional assessments to support RTS decision-making.

metadata.title: Female Team-Sport Athletes' Physical Fitness and Jump Performance Kinematics After Plyometric Jump Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plyometric jump training (PJT) can improve athletes' physical fitness across a range of sports and populations. Nonetheless, the role of PJT in adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics remains unclear, particularly given the increasing number of published, heterogeneous studies. OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to first examine the effectiveness of PJT in improving physical fitness and jump-performance kinematics in adult female team-sport athletes, and second, to provide evidence-based recommendations for PJT prescription for this population. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO databases up to March 2026. The included studies recruited healthy female team-sport athletes (mean age: ≥ 18 years), incorporated a PJT programme ≥ 2 weeks in duration, included comparator groups, and assessed athletes' physical fitness, jump performance, and/or kinematics. The risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Hedges' g effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were reported using a random-effects model for meta-analyses. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the participant characteristics (height, body mass, sport) and PJT programming variables (duration, frequency, total sessions, weekly total jumps). The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. RESULTS: Thirty-one articles were included (n = 609 participants), and 25 were meta-analysed. Two studies were categorised with high RoB (≤ 3 points), 20 studies achieved moderate RoB (4-5 points), and 9 studies achieved low RoB (≥ 6 points). Compared to controls, PJT improved countermovement jump (CMJ) height (ES = 0.550, p < 0.001), CMJ peak concentric velocity (ES = 0.623, p = 0.011), drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) (ES = 0.926, p = 0.001), DJ height (ES = 0.721, p = 0.002), 10 m sprint time (ES = 0.712, p = 0.032), 20 m sprint time (ES = 0.709, p < 0.001), 30 m sprint time (ES = 1.018, p = 0.001), non-linear (agility) Illinois test time (ES = 1.225, p < 0.001) and T test sprint time (ES = 0.965, p < 0.001). Compared to PJT ≤ 6 weeks, longer interventions favoured DJ RSI (p = 0.008), 10 m sprint time (p = 0.001), and Illinois agility test time (p < 0.001). Impact of heterogeneity (I2) remained low (≤ 0.06%) in five analyses and moderate in the other four analyses (≤ 73.1%). The certainty of evidence was considered low to moderate for the study outcomes. Two studies reported that a total of three participants possibly sustained an injury during PJT. CONCLUSIONS: Adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics improved after PJT when compared to the control condition, including CMJ height, CMJ peak concentric velocity, DJ RSI, linear sprint speed, and non-linear (agility) sprint speed. The improvements were particularly notable with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks). TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NERCY.

metadata.title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain. PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis. STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1. METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care (PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, satisfaction, adverse events, and costs. RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) (Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was maintained. CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

metadata.title: Acupuncture for postoperative pain management and functional recovery after total knee arthroplasty in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture for postoperative pain management and functional recovery in older adults following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating acupuncture or electroacupuncture for postoperative outcomes in adults undergoing TKA. Primary outcomes included pain intensity (Visual Analogue Scale [VAS]) and functional outcomes (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index [WOMAC], Hospital for Special Surgery [HSS] score, and range of motion). Secondary outcomes included analgesic consumption and adverse events. RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs involving 1037 participants were included. Acupuncture and electroacupuncture were associated with reduced postoperative pain (VAS: SMD = -1.08, 95% CI, -1.27 to -0.89; Z = 11.09; p < 0.00001) and improved functional outcomes (HSS: SMD = 1.39, 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.75; Z = 7.48; p < 0.00001). No serious adverse events were reported in the included studies. CONCLUSIONS: Acupuncture may provide beneficial effects on postoperative pain and selected functional outcomes after TKA in older adults. Given the multidisciplinary nature of postoperative recovery, these findings may be relevant to geriatric nursing care, particularly in pain assessment, rehabilitation coordination, and monitoring of recovery. However, the available evidence does not establish acupuncture as a nurse-led intervention.

metadata.title: Effects and Moderators of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) on Physiological Adaptations Among Team-Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
metadata.abstract: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is widely used in team sports, but the influence of participant and programme characteristics on physiological adaptations remains unclear. Five databases (Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CNKI) were searched initially on 25 April 2025 and updated on 21 December 2025. Mixed-effects models were used to estimate Hedges' g and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Forty-six studies involving 1204 athletes were included. Compared with regular sport-specific training alone, HIIT produced positive effects on maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max; g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.61, 0.92]), maximal aerobic power (g = 0.43, 95% CI [0.04, 0.82]), ventilatory threshold (g = 0.70, 95% CI [0.53, 0.88]), Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test performance (g = 1.02, 95% CI [0.76, 1.28]), and 30-s Wingate peak (g = 0.91, 95% CI [0.67, 1.16]) and mean power (g = 0.70, 95% CI [0.39, 1.01]). Effects on body composition were generally unclear. Mutually adjusted multivariable meta-regression identified no convincing evidence of differences in VO2max or Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test performance effects by sex or training level. Longer training duration was associated with greater VO2max effects. In exploratory analyses, model predictions indicated increases in VO2max of 2.56 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI [1.54, 3.58]) after approximately 5 weeks and 5.11 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI [3.32, 6.91]) after approximately 10 weeks. Shorter between-repetition recovery was associated with greater VO2max effects, although other programme variables were estimated imprecisely. Overall, adding HIIT to regular sport-specific training improves aerobic and anaerobic performance in trained team-sport athletes, whereas effects on body composition are limited. Associations involving programme characteristics should be interpreted cautiously because they were derived from study-level meta-regression. Trial Registration: PROSPERO Registration CRD42024609379.

metadata.title: Nitric oxide precursor interventions for post-exercise delayed onset muscle soreness: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) commonly follows high-intensity or unaccustomed exercise. Nitric oxide (NO) precursors may reduce DOMS, but their effects remain uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis to evaluate NO precursor interventions across recovery time points. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched to February 2026 for randomized controlled trials in healthy adults. Interventions were classified into four nodes: beetroot-derived nitrate, watermelon-derived citrulline, synthetic or isolated amino acid precursors (L-arginine and citrulline malate), and watermelon plus added citrulline. Random-effects network meta-analyses were conducted separately at 24, 48, and 72 h. Effects were expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); SUCRA rankings were exploratory. Risk of bias and evidence certainty were assessed using RoB 2 and CINeMA, with subgroup and sensitivity analyses examining robustness. RESULTS: Nineteen trials involving 356 participants were included. At 24 h, watermelon plus added citrulline (SMD = -0.97, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.31) and beetroot-derived nitrate (SMD = -0.67, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.20) significantly reduced DOMS vs. placebo. At 48 h, beetroot-derived nitrate was the only intervention with a significant benefit (SMD = -1.18, 95% CI -1.91 to -0.45). No active intervention differed significantly from placebo at 72 h, while evidence for differences between active interventions was limited, with only watermelon plus added citrulline showing a significant advantage over synthetic or isolated amino acid precursors at 24 h. Beetroot-derived nitrate significantly reduced DOMS vs. placebo in the trained subgroup but not in the untrained subgroup. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the findings, although the beetroot-derived nitrate estimate was sensitive to some restrictions related to the exercise-induced muscle damage model. CONCLUSION: NO precursor supplementation may reduce post-exercise DOMS at specific recovery time points, particularly with beetroot-derived nitrate and watermelon plus added citrulline. However, evidence for differences between active interventions remains limited, and the sparse network, substantial heterogeneity, and low certainty of evidence preclude firm clinical conclusions. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261373938, identifier: CRD420261373938.

metadata.title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight. OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss. METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA). RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min. CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

metadata.title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain. METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function). RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

metadata.title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA. METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year. RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups. CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

metadata.title: Patients Undergoing Proximal Hamstring Repair Have High Rates of Return to Work and Favorable Outcomes: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate return-to-work (RTW) rates and functional outcomes after surgical repair of proximal hamstring tendon avulsion injuries. METHODS: This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews. PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Scopus were searched in April 2025 for studies reporting RTW outcomes after surgical repair of proximal hamstring avulsions. Eligible studies involved human subjects undergoing open or endoscopic repair and reporting RTW rates or patient counts. No minimum follow-up duration was required. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, with discrepancies resolved by a third. Study quality was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies criteria. RESULTS: Six studies (229 patients) met inclusion criteria. Four studies reported an overall RTW rate ranging from 89% to 100%, whereas 2 studies stratified outcomes by Workers' Compensation (WC) status, showing lower RTW rates among WC patients (70.0%-86.3%) compared with non-WC patients (92.5%-94.1%). Return-to-sport rates, when reported, ranged from 58% to 100%. Study-level RTW and return-to-sport outcomes were summarized descriptively without pooled estimates because of heterogeneity in study design, surgical approach, injury chronicity, WC status, and outcome definitions. Complication rates were low overall, with retear or reoperation occurring in 0% to 5.8% of cases. Clinically relevant patient improvement thresholds were only reported in 1 study. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, most patients undergoing surgical repair for proximal hamstring avulsion injuries return to work with favorable functional outcomes and low complication rates. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level III and IV studies.

metadata.title: Management of Hand Injuries: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Surgical and Rehabilitation Strategies.
metadata.abstract: Management of traumatic hand injuries has evolved substantially with advances in anesthesia, tendon repair, biological adjuncts, fracture fixation, and rehabilitation. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary evidence on surgical and rehabilitation strategies for improving functional recovery and reducing complications after acute hand trauma. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261320700). PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for studies published from January 2000 to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials and prospective comparative studies evaluating contemporary strategies for flexor or extensor tendon injuries and metacarpal or phalangeal fractures were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Of 3417 records identified, 354 duplicates were removed and 3063 records were screened. Following full-text assessment, 23 studies were included. Evidence supported the use of wide-awake local anesthesia no tourniquet (WALANT) as a safe alternative to general anesthesia, although functional superiority was not consistent across trials. Acellular dermal matrices, biological amnion, hydrogels, hyaluronic acid, and other adjuncts showed potential for reducing adhesions and improving tendon gliding. Early active mobilization and place-and-hold protocols produced favorable functional outcomes, while relative motion extension orthoses improved early function after extensor tendon repair. Smartphone-assisted rehabilitation improved adherence. Headless compression screws facilitated earlier functional recovery in selected metacarpal fractures, while multistrand tendon repairs provided sufficient strength for early mobilization. Contemporary hand injury management increasingly integrates WALANT, robust tendon repair, anti-adhesion adjuncts, early active rehabilitation, modern orthoses, and digital adherence tools. However, heterogeneity and variable risk of bias across studies warrant cautious interpretation and further high-quality comparative research.

metadata.title: Non-Surgical Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. As many patients seek to avoid surgery, a synthesis of conservative treatment options is clinically relevant for evidence-based management. METHODS: A structured PubMed literature search was conducted through December 15, 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating nonsurgical interventions for knee OA. Extracted outcomes included pain, function, safety, and comparative effectiveness across reported follow-up durations. RESULTS: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) has a favorable safety profile and may delay progression to total knee arthroplasty, though benefits over placebo are modest and guideline recommendations inconsistent. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) improves pain and function and may outperform HA, although outcomes vary with preparation methods and study quality. Autologous conditioned serum and dextrose prolotherapy demonstrate symptomatic benefit, whereas corticosteroid injections primarily provide short-term relief. Disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs), including sprifermin, lorecivivint, LNA043, cathepsin-K inhibition, ADAMTS-5 inhibition, and repurposed metabolic agents such as metformin, are emerging investigational strategies with variable structural and symptomatic results. Early evidence suggests mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies may improve outcomes but remain investigational. Core conservative measures, including exercise therapy, physical therapy, and weight reduction, consistently reduce pain and improve function. Assistive devices and valgus bracing provide additional symptomatic and biomechanical benefit. Among device-based interventions, cooled radiofrequency ablation offers durable pain relief compared with HA or corticosteroids, while sustained acoustic medicine and extracorporeal shockwave therapy show functional improvement; evidence for pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is mixed. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provide effective analgesia with reduced systemic risk. CONCLUSION: Non-surgical management of knee OA should follow a stepwise approach, with rehabilitation and weight optimization as first-line therapy, selective injection- and device-based options for persistent symptoms, and timely surgical referral when disability remains refractory. Future progress will depend on standardized protocols and higher-quality long-term comparative trials to improve treatment selection and disease modification.

metadata.title: Physical activity levels two years after total knee arthroplasty and preoperative patient characteristics: a secondary analysis of the MOVE randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: At one year after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), patients are less physically active than age-matched peers, but physical activity (PA) trajectories two years after TKA are unclear. This study examined PA levels from baseline to two years post-TKA, quantified return to baseline PA levels over time, and evaluated associations between baseline participant characteristics and post-TKA PA levels. METHODS: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Participants (n = 135) aged 50 to 85 years undergoing primary unilateral TKA wore accelerometers preoperatively and 10 weeks, six months, and two years post-TKA to characterize light PA, moderate-vigorous PA (MVPA), and steps/day. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize PA levels. Repeated measures models estimated PA levels over time. The percentage of participants who returned to or exceeded baseline PA levels over time was quantified. Multivariate logistic regressions modeled return to baseline PA levels over time to evaluate associations with baseline participant characteristics. All models controlled for age, sex, and treatment group. RESULTS: There was an increase of 8% steps/day and 0.75% MVPA from baseline to two years post-TKA. At two years post-TKA, 54.2, 53.1, and 55.6% of participants returned to baseline light PA, MVPA, and steps/day levels. Higher baseline PA levels were associated with lower odds of returning to baseline levels at all timepoints for MVPA (10 weeks odds ratio (95% confidence interval): 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84); six months: 0.55 (0.40 to 0.76); two years: 0.52 (0.36 to 0.75)), as well as light PA and steps/day (all P-values < 0.05). Baseline body mass index, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index scores, and Functional Comorbidity Index were associated inconsistently with PA levels. CONCLUSION: While on average, PA levels increased from baseline to two years post-TKA, participants who have higher baseline PA levels had reduced odds of returning to the same level. These findings suggest TKA and current rehabilitation may not fully address PA, and additional support (e.g., behavioral guidance or tailored rehabilitation) may be needed.

metadata.title: The effect of adding whole-body electromyostimulation to hip and knee strengthening exercises on pain, muscle strength, and function in women with patellofemoral pain syndrome: A randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Strength training is a key treatment for patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). Although conventional strengthening exercises offer important benefits, whole-body electromyostimulation (WB-EMS) may provide complementary advantages; however, its additive effects in PFPS remain unclear. PURPOSE: This study investigated the short-term effects of adding WB-EMS to hip and knee strengthening exercises on pain and self-reported function in women with PFPS. It also assessed immediate post-treatment effects on muscle strength and objective function. METHODS: In this single-blind randomized controlled trial, 36 women with unilateral PFPS were randomized to strengthening exercises alone (control) or combined WB-EMS and strengthening exercises (intervention). All performed strengthening exercises three times weekly over 7 weeks (21 sessions); the intervention group additionally received WB-EMS twice weekly (14 sessions). Primary outcomes - worst pain in the previous week (visual analog scale (VAS)) and knee-related symptoms and function (Kujala scale) - were assessed at baseline, 7 weeks, and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes (muscle strength, step-down test repetitions) were measured at baseline and 7 weeks. RESULTS: Significant group-by-time interactions were found for VAS (F(2,33)=6.41, p = .003, ηp2 = 0.16) and the Kujala scale (F(2,33)=3.86, p = .026, ηp2 = 0.15). VAS was significantly lower in the intervention group at 3 months (mean difference [MD] = -7.64, 95% CI: -9.36 to -3.16, p = .014). Kujala scores were significantly higher at 7 weeks (MD = 5.61, 95% CI: 2.33 to 8.88, p = .001) and 3 months (MD = 7.32, 95% CI: 3.82 to 10.83, p < .001). Significant interactions were also shown for step-down test repetitions (F(1,33)=10.33, p = .003, ηp2 = 0.23), knee extensor strength (F(1,33)=8.06, p = .008, ηp2 = 0.19), and knee flexor strength (F(1,33)=9.21, p = .005, ηp2 = 0.21). CONCLUSION: Adding WB-EMS to strengthening exercises may improve pain, knee muscle strength, and function in women with unilateral PFPS. Larger, adequately powered trials with appropriate blinding and longer objective follow-up are warranted.

metadata.title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

metadata.title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment. DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively. RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

metadata.title: Effects of Exercise Type and Duration on Pain, Function, and Quality of Life in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review With Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the effects of aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, and combined interventions on pain, function, and quality of life (QoL) in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA) at the short term (≤12 weeks) and long term (>12 weeks). DESIGN: Intervention systematic review with Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA). LITERATURE SEARCH: MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PEDro, AMED, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception until July 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials of patients with knee OA that evaluated exercise interventions aimed at improving pain, function, and QoL. DATA SYNTHESIS: Using random-effects models, the NMA synthesized effect sizes and ranked interventions by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), with evidence certainty assessed via the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. RESULTS: Thirty-five trials (n = 3808 patients) were included. For pain, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect among the interventions (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.937, low certainty). For function, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect estimates (SMD = -0.590, low certainty), followed by long-term aerobic exercise (SMD = -0.540, very low certainty). Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect (SMD = 0.663, low certainty) for improving QoL. CONCLUSION: Aerobic and resistance exercise, alone or in combination, and delivered over the short- or long-term, improved pain, function, and QoL for patients with knee OA. Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had clinically meaningful improvements for pain, with relatively favorable effects on function and QoL. Evidence regarding the clinical significance of long-term exercise interventions was limited. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(11):724-734. Epub 24 July 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.13875.

metadata.title: First-Hand Experience and the Value of Telerehabilitation for Chronic Knee Pain: A Discrete Choice Experiment Nested in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess whether first-hand experience of receiving physical therapy via telerehabilitation affected patient preferences and willingness to pay for telerehabilitation. DESIGN: This study used a discrete choice experiment nested within a randomized controlled trial. METHODS: We recruited 319 Australian adults aged 45 years or over, with chronic knee pain consistent with osteoarthritis, who had completed a clinical trial where they were randomized to receive physical therapy via telerehabilitation or in-person. Participants were presented hypothetical scenarios and asked to choose between physical therapy delivered via telerehabilitation or in-person. Each scenario presented seven attributes of consultations at varying levels. Data were analyzed using a generalized multinomial logit and latent class models. RESULTS: There were 164 participants from the in-person trial arm (80% of those randomized) and 155 from the telerehabilitation arm (82% of those randomized) who participated. Participants in the telerehabilitation arm (ie, with first-hand experience of telerehabilitation) were willing to pay AU$ 87.49 (95% confidence interval: 72.83, 102.14) more than people in the in-person arm for telerehabilitation consultations (all other attributes fixed at reference values for categorical variables and at mean values for continuous variables). Four subgroups were identified. In the telerehabilitation arm, 105 (68% of 155) participants preferred telerehabilitation, and 50 (32%) preferred in-person consultations. In the in-person arm, 63 (39% of 164) held a strong preference for in-person consultations, and 101 (61%) had a mild preference for in-person consultations. CONCLUSION: People with first-hand experience using telerehabilitation for physical therapy expressed a greater willingness to use and pay for it than people who experienced in-person care. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(11):735-744. Epub 23 September 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14073.

metadata.title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited. METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05. RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected. CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).

metadata.title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2. RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

metadata.title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS). METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates. RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

metadata.title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting. METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed. RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low. CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

metadata.title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
metadata.abstract: CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians. EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing. STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5. RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

metadata.title: Long Head of Biceps Tenodesis: Fixation Constructs and Tenodesis Level-A Narrative Review.
metadata.abstract: Disorders of the long head of the biceps tendon (LHBT) are a common source of anterior shoulder pain and are frequently encountered in patients undergoing shoulder surgery. Biceps tenodesis has gained popularity because it addresses biceps-related symptoms while preserving muscle contour and function. This narrative review summarizes contemporary evidence on LHBT tenodesis, with particular emphasis on fixation constructs and tenodesis level, and integrates current evidence into a practical framework for surgical decision-making. A literature review was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar, incorporating clinical studies, biomechanical investigations, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating tenodesis techniques, fixation methods, outcomes, and complications. Current evidence indicates that top-of-groove, suprapectoral, and subpectoral tenodesis can provide favorable pain and functional outcomes, with comparative clinical studies generally demonstrating limited clinically meaningful differences between levels. Subpectoral tenodesis may more completely address groove-related pathology but is associated with approach-specific risks, whereas biomechanical differences among interference screws, suture anchors, cortical buttons, and onlay constructs have not consistently translated into differences in clinical outcomes. Rehabilitation protocols vary considerably and are commonly influenced by concomitant procedures. The available evidence is limited by heterogeneous techniques and patient populations, relatively few randomized comparisons, and limited long-term follow-up. Accordingly, no single tenodesis level or fixation construct can currently be considered universally superior. Patient-specific factors, groove pathology, surgical context, and the strength and applicability of the available evidence should inform individualized surgical decision-making.

metadata.title: The Effect of Acute Beetroot Juice and Caffeine Supplementation on Specific Judo Performance During a Simulated Competition Day in Judo Athletes.
metadata.abstract: Beetroot juice (BJ) and caffeine (CAF) are well-established ergogenic aids for exercise performance. However, little is known about their efficacy and interaction within the specific context of a judo competition day. This study investigated the acute effects of BJ, CAF, and their combination (BJCAF) on judo-specific performance across a simulated competition day. Using a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design, 35 competitive judo athletes (age 23 ± 5 years; body mass 74 ± 13 kg) completed 4 sessions (BJ, CAF, BJCAF, and placebo), each consisting of 5 trials of judo randori and a Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT), followed by neuromuscular and cognitive assessments. Compared with placebo, CAF enhanced SJFT performance, neuromuscular function, and cognition in trials 1-3 but not in trial 5 (p < 0.05). Conversely, BJ improved these same metrics in trial 5 (p < 0.05). BJCAF enhanced SJFT performance across trials 1-3 and 5, cognitive functions in trials 1, 2, and 4, and neuromuscular performance in all trials (p < 0.05). Importantly, in trial 5, both BJ and BJCAF conditions yielded improved SJFT performance, neuromuscular function, and cognitive outcomes compared to CAF alone (p < 0.05). The results demonstrate that the ergogenic effect of CAF was not maintained throughout the simulated competition day, whereas BJ provided late-stage benefits. Co-ingestion effectively counteracted the later-session decline observed with CAF alone while maintaining its early advantages. This highlights the importance of considering temporal dynamics and metabolic costs when designing nutritional strategies for multi-bout, high-intensity sports tournaments such as judo.

metadata.title: Quadriceps Tendon Autograft for Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Has No Difference in Short-Term Clinical Outcomes Between All-Soft Tissue Versus Tendon-Bone Grafts: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare clinical outcomes and complications after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with all-soft tissue quadriceps tendon (ST-QT) versus quadriceps tendon-bone (QT-B) autograft. METHODS: A systematic review was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines by searching PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library to identify studies directly comparing outcomes of primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with ST-QT versus QT-B autograft. Outcomes included rates of graft failure and other complications, patient-reported outcomes, return to sport, anteroposterior knee laxity, pivot shift testing, and the Objective International Knee Documentation Committee score. RESULTS: Five studies (1 Level II, 4 Level III) met the inclusion criteria, including a total of 996 knees undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with ST-QT autograft and 1279 with QT-B autograft. Mean age at surgery ranged from 20.3 to 31.7 years. Minimum follow-up time ranged from 12.0 to 24.0 months. The overall percentage of men ranged from 48.8% to 84.6%. Graft failure ranged from 2.4% to 7.6% of patients in the ST-QT autograft group and 3.3% to 6.4% in the QT-B autograft group. No study found a significant difference in graft failure rates between the 2 groups. Intraoperative patellar fracture occurred in 2 cases overall, both in the QT-B group. No studies found a significant difference in return to sport between groups. One study found significantly better Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score subscale scores in the ST-QT group. One study found a significantly greater proportion of ST-QT patients showing a positive pivot shift postoperatively. No other significant differences were found for the remaining patient-reported outcomes between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Current comparative evidence suggests ST-QT and QT-B autografts for primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction yield similar short- to midterm outcomes, though limited studies and follow-up warrant cautious interpretation. Patellar fracture remains an uncommon QT-B risk. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

metadata.title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
metadata.abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

metadata.title: From Signal to Biological Meaning: A Systematic Review of Construct-Validity Evidence for External Training Load Metrics in Sport.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: External training load (ETL) metrics describe external work but often imply metabolic demand, neuromuscular load, tissue stress, fatigue, or adaptation. These interpretations require construct-validity evidence beyond device accuracy or reliability. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Academic Search Ultimate from inception to March 2026; final searches were on 1 March, except Embase on 7 March. Eligible peer-reviewed English studies evaluated an ETL indicator and its interpreted construct in athletes or physically active participants. Reports limited to technical accuracy, reliability, measurement error, or descriptive monitoring were excluded. We adjudicated one page-anchored construct-evidence chain per study. Measurement-property analyses used review-adapted COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments (COSMIN); prediction models used the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool plus Artificial Intelligence (PROBAST+AI); other designs used Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools. Conceptual and methodological heterogeneity across metrics, target constructs, comparators, and study designs precluded meaningful meta-analysis; therefore, we used evidence maps and narrative synthesis. RESULTS: Forty-six studies contributed 46 primary evidence chains. Main study samples ranged from 7 to 71 participants, with smaller analysis-specific subsamples; most studies included only men. Construct attribution was explicit in 14 studies and explicit but qualified in 26; four were implicit but qualified and two reverse-target. Thirteen studies (28%) used a direct construct-matched criterion. Alternative proxies supported 16 studies (35%), condition or group contrasts 11 (24%), and mixed routes six (13%). General exercise intensity was the most frequent construct family (15 studies, 33%). Appraisal identified common limitations in hypotheses testing and analysis. Nineteen studies (41%) explicitly distinguished technical performance from construct interpretation, and 12 (26%) explicitly justified comparator selection. CONCLUSIONS: Most ETL metrics were supported as descriptions of external movement, work, or exposure rather than direct indicators of biological demand or response. Biological interpretations require an explicit construct, plausible mechanism, directional hypothesis, and construct-matched reference. Heterogeneity and methodological limitations reduce confidence in biological interpretations.

metadata.title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included. RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed. CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

metadata.title: Return to Sport After Foot and Ankle Surgery Is Inconsistently Defined and Assessed: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To conduct a systematic review of return-to-sport (RTS) definitions in the orthopaedic literature, addressing common operative athletic foot and ankle pathologies including ankle instability, Achilles tendon ruptures or tendinopathy, and fifth metatarsal fractures. METHODS: A systematic review was performed in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Cochrane, Embase, Medline, and CINAHL databases were searched for studies published through March 2024. Inclusion criteria were studies in which subjects were involved in some level of sports and received surgery for 1 of 3 common sports-related injuries: ankle instability, Achilles tendinopathy, and fifth metatarsal fracture. The primary outcome was each study's definition of RTS. RESULTS: There were 145 articles that met all inclusion criteria. Of these, 73 articles investigated ankle instability, 56 investigated Achilles tendinopathy, and 16 investigated fifth metatarsal fracture. Seventy-nine articles (54.5%) had an unclear definition of RTS with 66 articles (45.5%) reporting a precise definition. Sixty-four articles (44.1%) provided an isolated binary metric reporting whether a patient returned to sport or failed to provide a method for determining the timepoint for RTS. Thirty-eight (26.2%) of the articles used an objective start criterion (e.g., resumption of competition), followed by custom (n = 27, 18.6%) and standardized patient-reported questionnaire use (n = 21, 14.5%). CONCLUSIONS: Most articles included in this systematic review did not provide an explicit definition of RTS or a clearly defined assessment methodology. When specified, RTS was assessed using objective events, custom questionnaires, or standardized patient-reported outcome measures, highlighting substantial heterogeneity in both RTS definitions and assessment approaches across foot and ankle literature. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level I to IV studies.

metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION OR BACKGROUND: The anaerobic threshold (AnT) marks the transition between heavy and severe exercise intensity domains and guides training prescription and performance monitoring. Criterion methods (blood lactate and gas exchange) are accurate but invasive, costly, or impractical outside laboratories, prompting the search for noninvasive surrogates. This review evaluates the validity of these estimation procedures rather than the underlying physiology. SOURCES OF DATA: MEDLINE (via PubMed) was searched from inception without language restrictions, supplemented by reference-list and citation searching. Eligible studies compared noninvasive AnT indices, including heart rate variability (HRV; including detrended fluctuation analysis [DFA] α1), cardiac repolarization instability, heart rate deflection/field slope-variation methods, critical power (CP)/ critical speed (CS), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), the talk test, and machine-learning (ML) models, with criterion standards. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Eighty-eight reports were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed. AREAS OF AGREEMENT: DFA α1, NIRS breakpoints, and CP/CS show strong associations with laboratory criteria and increasing field applicability through wearables. Accuracy and feasibility trade-offs require method selection according to the threshold, sport, and required precision. AREAS OF CONTROVERSY: Correlation indicates group-level association rather than individual agreement; Bland-Altman and reliability analyses are more informative for substitution. Criterion standards are not interchangeable, and heart rate deflection is not consistently identifiable. Evidence in female athletes remains limited. GROWING POINTS: Multimodal wearables integrating HRV, muscle oxygenation, and running power with ML may improve field-based threshold estimation. AREAS FOR DEVELOPING RESEARCH: Priorities include standardized reporting, transparent bias assessment, female-athlete validation, and broader systematic and meta-analytic synthesis.

metadata.title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance. METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes. RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939). CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.
