metadata.title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

metadata.title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes. METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses. RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC. CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

metadata.title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases. METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs. RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15). CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

metadata.title: Five-Year Outcomes and Return to Sport After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in Young Patients With Minimal (<10%) or No Glenoid Bone Loss.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Arthroscopic Bankart repair is commonly used to address anterior instability in adolescents and young adults with no or minimal bone loss. However, failure rates remain high, particularly in high-risk populations. PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate clinical outcomes, return-to-sport (RTS) rates, and predictors of failure after arthroscopic Bankart repair in patients ≤24 years of age with minimal glenoid bone loss. It was hypothesized that patients would demonstrate favorable outcomes, low recurrence rates, and high RTS rates, and smaller distance-to-dislocation (DTD) measurements, and contact sports participation would be associated with failure. STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. METHODS: The data of patients with anterior shoulder instability and minimal bone loss (<10%) who underwent primary arthroscopic Bankart repair between 2006 and 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. Remplissage was not performed. Data collected included preoperative instability events, patient-reported outcome measures, satisfaction, radiographic measurements (glenoid bone loss, glenoid track, and DTD), and RTS outcomes. Failure was defined as re-dislocation or recurrent instability requiring surgery. RESULTS: A total of 130 patients were evaluated; 18 were excluded, leaving 112. Of these, 96 patients (85.7%) were available for the final follow-up (mean age, 19.9 ± 3.1 years; mean follow-up, 68.4 ± 42.7 months). All clinical outcomes improved significantly (P < .05) except for the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey Mental Component Summary score. The median satisfaction score was 9 (IQR, 8-10). Participation in contact sports was associated with failure, while other risk factors were not. RTS was achieved by 96.1% of patients; however, only 57.1% returned to their preinjury level. Fewer preoperative dislocation events were associated with successful return to full activity (P = .04). The recurrence rate was 33.3%, and revision surgery was required in 19 patients (19.8%). CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic Bankart repair was associated with high rates of recurrence and revision surgery in a series of patients ≤24 years of age without glenoid bone loss. In those who did not require revision surgery, clinical outcomes and RTS rates were high. Contact sports participation was associated with failure. A greater number of preoperative instability events negatively influence RTS outcomes. Arthroscopic Bankart repair in this population is safe and has a low complication rate, but the failure rate remains considerable.

metadata.title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
metadata.abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

metadata.title: Multimodal rehabilitation interventions reduce pain in dogs with osteoarthritis, regardless of enrollment in formal in-clinic or outpatient rehabilitation.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objective was to determine the effects of multimodal rehabilitation interventions on Canine Brief Pain Inventory (CBPI) pain scores in dogs diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA), and to determine whether effects differed between formal in-clinic versus outpatient rehabilitation. ANIMALS AND PROCEDURE: Medical records from between 2022 and 2024 were reviewed for dogs with OA that were presented to a rehabilitation specialist. Each dog's caregiver completed a CBPI at both the initial evaluation and 1st follow-up visit. Dogs were allocated into 2 groups: those that received in-clinic rehabilitation and those that received outpatient interventions. Both groups received customized, multimodal plans to address their OA signs. Pain severity scores (PSS), pain interference scores (PIS), and overall interference scores were compared between groups. A 2-sample Student's t-test or a Fisher's exact test was used to compare groups, with a statistical significance level of 0.05. RESULTS: A total of 79 dogs were included in the study. There were no differences between dogs enrolled in in-clinic rehabilitation versus outpatient rehabilitation for sex, age, weight, or body condition score (P = 0.541, P = 0.26, P = 0.58, P = 0.33, respectively). The PSS and PIS had improved at the 1st recheck in both groups (in-clinic: P = 0.01 and P = 0.03; outpatient: P = 0.03 and P = 0.03, respectively). CONCLUSION AND CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Owner-perceived pain decreased in all dogs, whether they were enrolled in formal in-clinic rehabilitation or not. This was attributed to customized interventions, including rehabilitation, pain management, and weight management. Our results corroborated reports that multimodal OA management plans, including rehabilitation interventions, ameliorate symptoms of OA in humans. Given the high prevalence of canine OA, this study supported the beneficial effects of multimodal rehabilitation interventions on the well-being of osteoarthritic dogs.

metadata.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases. METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05). RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047). CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management. KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

metadata.title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR). METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction. RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR. CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

metadata.title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
metadata.abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

metadata.title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions. METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot. RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance. CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

metadata.title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited. METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored. RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects. CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

metadata.title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
metadata.abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

metadata.title: Effect of Pulsed Electromagnetic Stimulation on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: The effect of pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy on muscle performance and serum creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Mb) values - the biomarkers of muscle damage in experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) - has yet to be investigated. PEMF therapy is known to be effective to reduce muscle pain, muscle recovery time, fatigue but not to increase muscle force production. The study aimed to compare the effect of PEMF and sham therapy on experimentally induced DOMS in sedentary undergraduate college students. HYPOTHESIS: PEMF therapy would improve pain, pressure pain threshold (PPT), functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration compared with the sham intervention. STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, participant- and assessor-blinded, sham-controlled study. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2. METHODS: This study was conducted at Pamukkale University Sarayköy Vocational School. A total of 52 healthy sedentary people received 3 consecutive days of active (Experimental group, n = 26) or sham (Sham group, n = 26) PEMF therapy 24 hours after DOMS induction with a drop-jump protocol. Pain intensity, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration were assessed at baseline, 24 hours and 72 hours after DOMS induction protocol. RESULTS: The drop-jump protocol induced DOMS successfully in both groups (P < 0.05). All outcome measures were improved in the experimental group (P < 0.05). Mean change scores of PPT (P = 0.53), functional performance (P = 0.10), serum CK (P = 0.38), and Mb concentrations (P = 0.08) were not significantly different between baseline and 72 hours in the sham group. Statistically significant decreases in Mb concentrations were determined in the sham group (P = 0.001). CONCLUSION: Compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration. The duration of PEMF therapy was sufficient to resolve the PPT, functional performance, and serum CK and Mb concentrations associated with DOMS. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study adds to existing knowledge in showing that, compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration.

metadata.title: Spatial transcriptomics in immune-mediated necrotising myopathy uncovers a specific necrotic signature related to immune-driven fibrosis.
metadata.abstract: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathies (IMNM) are characterised by muscle fibre necrosis, complement deposits around non-necrotic fibres, and macrophage infiltrates. Patients experience muscle damage with fibro-fatty replacement, leading to poor strength recovery, but the pathogenesis remains unclear. To investigate IMNM pathogenesis, we applied spatial transcriptomics on myositis muscle biopsies and integrated the results with published single-nucleus transcriptomic data. This combined approach enabled analysis of gene expression with spatial localisation in the muscle. Inflammatory, fibrotic, regenerative, and lipid metabolism-related signatures were identified in IMNM, distinct from other myositis, with specific distribution in necrotic and peri-necrotic regions. A unique subtype of immune-driven fibroblasts expressing SFRP4 was enriched in IMNM necrotic areas. These cells carried a strong proportion of IMNM-enriched pathological signatures, notably a complement-linked 'tumour-like' inflammatory fibroblast signature and a specific interferon response, characterised by the expression of metallothioneins. Peri-necrotic areas were characterised by pathological muscle signatures carrying interferon response and FABP4+ metabolically dysfunctional signatures. In conclusion, IMNM necrotic muscle areas are linked to a specific SFRP4-expressing fibroblast subtype interacting with macrophages, potentially driving the pathological muscle phenotype and contributing to inflammation, fibro-fatty replacement, and strength loss.

metadata.title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects. METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented. RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program. CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

metadata.title: Weightbearing CT in the Evaluation of Athletic Foot and Ankle Injuries.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Subtle foot and ankle injuries in athletes, including syndesmotic sprains, ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, osteochondral lesions of the talus, and proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, may be underestimated or misclassified on conventional imaging. This review summarizes the current role of weightbearing CT (WBCT) in their evaluation, focusing on quantitative parameters, recent technical advances, and their potential influence on clinical decision-making. RECENT FINDINGS: Recent evidence has shifted WBCT from qualitative assessment toward reproducible three-dimensional quantification. Volumetric assessment and distance mapping improve characterization of syndesmotic instability, while external-rotation stress can reveal abnormalities not evident during neutral standing. In the midfoot, triplanar realignment and side-to-side comparison improve the reliability of Lisfranc measurements and support detection of subtle instability. Distance mapping permits reproducible quantification of osteochondral lesion surface area, depth, and volume and may improve consistency in surgical planning. WBCT has also characterized sport-specific alignment patterns and a morphologic and bone-density phenotype associated with proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures. Semiautomated segmentation and deep-learning methods may further reduce observer dependence and analysis time. WBCT provides three-dimensional measurements under physiologic load that complement clinical examination and conventional imaging in selected athletic foot and ankle conditions. Its greatest current value lies in characterizing subtle instability, malalignment, and osseous morphology when these findings may alter treatment planning. However, most available evidence is retrospective and derived from symptomatic or injured cohorts. Prospective studies are needed to validate diagnostic thresholds, determine whether WBCT-derived parameters predict injury or outcomes, and define their role in routine athletic screening and return-to-sport decision-making.

metadata.title: The Role of Physical Preparation in Motorsport Athletes Across Different Vehicle Types: A Narrative Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite motorsport's widespread appeal, early performance models did not consider drivers as athletes, and even drivers often struggled with this classification, which historically contributed to their exclusion from research focused on athletic performance. Slowly but steadily, this paradigm has been changing. PURPOSE: To review the evolution of physical conditioning in land-based motorsports and to examine the specific physiological and physical demands imposed on drivers by different vehicle types. A narrative review was conducted to synthesize historical perspectives, physiological demands, and training approaches in motorsport. Peer-reviewed studies, practical reports, opinion articles, and relevant online materials were analyzed to describe the evolution of the physical conditioning required across racing categories. The physical demands in motorsports are characterized by sustained cardiovascular strain, significant neuromuscular loading, large and sustained G-force exposure, and pronounced thermal stress. These demands vary according to vehicle type. Closed-wheel drivers are particularly exposed to prolonged heat stress and require comprehensive muscular endurance and thermoregulatory adaptation. Open-wheel drivers experience large G-forces, demanding exceptional neck and lower-limb strength. Two-wheel riders require enhanced handgrip strength, dynamic neuromuscular control, and high levels of aerobic capacity. CONCLUSIONS: Tailored conditioning programs addressing the distinct physiological, neuromuscular, and thermoregulatory demands of each motorsport category are closely linked to performance and safety. Further systematic evaluation of the empirical evidence is necessary to enhance the ecological validity of training recommendations and strengthen their application in competitive motorsport.

metadata.title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults. METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions. RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h. CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

metadata.title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
metadata.abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

metadata.title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
metadata.abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

metadata.title: The gut-muscle-joint axis in osteoarthritis: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic perspectives.
metadata.abstract: Emerging evidence highlights a complex crosstalk between the gut microbiota, musculoskeletal tissues, and the joint microenvironment, revealing osteoarthritis (OA) as a systemic disorder rather than a localized cartilage disease. The gut-muscle-joint interaction integrates microbial dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation to influence cartilage homeostasis, muscle strength, and neuromuscular stability. Building upon previously described gut-osteoarthritis and gut-muscle interactions, the Gut-Muscle-Joint (GMJ) axis is presented as an integrative framework linking intestinal permeability, microbial metabolites, systemic inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular health, skeletal muscle function, and joint integrity. Perturbations in this axis amplify oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix degradation across musculoskeletal tissues. Understanding GMJ axis-driven mechanisms offers novel preventive and therapeutic strategies that target microbiome restoration, metabolic reprogramming, and neuromuscular health through probiotics, postbiotics, AMPK-SIRT1 activators, and structured exercise. This integrative perspective positions the GMJ axis as a unifying framework for intervention, enabling precision approaches to preserve joint function, reduce sarcopenia, and attenuate OA progression.

metadata.title: Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.
metadata.abstract: We read with interest the recent article by Barrera Uso et al. on early arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The study provides clinically relevant evidence that AMI at 30 days strongly predicts persistence at 60 days. We suggest, however, that this finding should be interpreted as a prognostic association rather than evidence that 30-day AMI is the dominant biological determinant of subsequent inhibition. We also discuss the timing of postoperative assessment, noting that evaluation at 30 days is appropriate for studying persistence but less informative regarding the initial pathophysiological development of AMI. The Scientific Anterior Cruciate Ligament Network International (SANTI) classification has demonstrated excellent reliability in anterior cruciate ligament populations, although its generalizability to TKA remains to be specifically established. Finally, the absence of objective functional and patient-reported outcomes limits interpretation of the clinical significance of persistent AMI. Overall, the study identifies an important clinical phenotype and useful prognostic markers while leaving the underlying mechanisms of persistence to be further clarified.

metadata.title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
metadata.abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

metadata.title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol. METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength. RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status. CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants. KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

metadata.title: Exostosis of the sustentaculum tali causing tibiotarsal joint pathology in a Standardbred racehorse trotter.
metadata.abstract: This report describes a novel case of exostosis on the medial aspect of the sustentaculum tali, (ST) associated with tibiotarsal joint (TTJ) pathology, without involvement of the tarsal sheath or lateral digital flexor tendon. A 5-year-old Standardbred gelding was presented with right TTJ effusion and exercise-induced hind-limb lameness. Diagnostic imaging identified a columnar periosteal proliferation on the medial ST, accompanied by synovial effusion and joint capsule thickening; however, the tarsal sheath and lateral digital flexor tendon remained unremarkable. Although TTJ arthroscopy confirmed synovitis, it did not allow visualization of the exostosis. The lesion was successfully excised via an ultrasound-guided extra-articular surgical approach. Postoperative management included a structured rehabilitation program, resulting in a return to full-speed training by Day 76 with no recurrence of lameness. Follow-up evaluations demonstrated improved performance and complete resolution of TTJ effusion and associated swelling. This case highlighted the importance of multimodal imaging in identifying extra-synovial lesions of the ST and supported ultrasound-guided extra-articular removal as an effective surgical option for ST exostosis. Although the underlying cause of the lesion was uncertain, subclinical trauma was considered a likely contributing factor. Key clinical message: The ST is a horizontal bony projection on the plantaromedial aspect of the calcaneus. Due to its minimal soft-tissue coverage, it is particularly vulnerable to external trauma and subsequent osseous proliferation. Exostosis of the ST may result in impingement of the plantaromedial pouch of the tarsocrural (tibiotarsal) joint, contributing to joint irritation and secondary pathology. Accurate diagnosis and effective case management rely on the combined use of radiography and ultrasonography, which together enable detailed assessment of both osseous changes and associated soft-tissue structures.

metadata.title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
metadata.abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

metadata.title: Immediate effect of verbal cues on ACL injury relevant Knee loading during 180° and 90° cutting maneuvers in female university soccer and basketball athletes.
metadata.abstract: Young female athletes possess a high risk of rupturing their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). High external peak knee abduction moments (pKAM) are a likely key risk factor for non-contact ACL injuries. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of performance-based movement feedback on pKAM during cutting maneuvers in female university athletes. Thirty-four female university soccer and basketball athletes completed preplanned 180° and 90° cutting trials while ground reaction forces and kinematics were simultaneously captured. Participants immediately received verbal cues targeting foot strike angle, foot progression angle, or trunk lean angle based on their performance. Athletes then repeated the trials post-feedback. Changes in pKAM between baseline and post-feedback trials were analyzed. Soccer and basketball athletes who received the FOOTstrike-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM for both cutting tasks (Soccer: 180°; -0.21 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.92; 90°; -0.28 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 1.16. Basketball: 180°; -0.07 Nm/kg, p = 0.02, d = 0.76; 90°; -0.30 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.82). The FOOTpro-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM during the 180° cut for soccer athletes (-0.10 Nm/kg, p = 0.01, d = 0.60), but not basketball. The TRUNKlean cue did not significantly affect pKAM for either sport. Individual feedback targeting forefoot landings and neutral foot progression angles can elicit immediate technique change and reduce ACL injury relevant knee loading during cutting maneuvers.

metadata.title: Facilitators and Barriers to Treatment Access and Use in Black Individuals With Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Qualitative Study.
metadata.abstract: CONTEXT: Individuals with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury are at high risk of knee osteoarthritis. Black individuals with osteoarthritis have worse pain and disability than White individuals. Racial disparities in ACL treatment use (ACL reconstruction and physical therapy) may contribute to disparities in long-term osteoarthritis-related disability. However, factors influencing ACL injury disparities are unknown. We explored facilitators and barriers to treatment access and use in Black individuals with ACL injury. DESIGN: Qualitative (semistructured interviews). METHODS: We included Black or African American individuals who self-reported ACL injury up to 5 years prior to recruitment, no longer seeking care for the injury, and 16-50 years old. We conducted one-on-one semistructured interviews and topics included facilitators and barriers to care, perceived communication, medical trust, and perceived discrimination. We used a reflexive thematic analysis approach to analyze the interviews. RESULTS: We included 10 participants (age 21-49 y, 8 women). We generated 4 themes: (1) path to diagnosis, (2) patient approach to treatment, (3) patient-provider interactions, and (4) life demands. ACL injury recovery was often complex with frustrations particularly common during the diagnosis process due to lack of an accurate diagnosis and poor communication on next steps. Participants took various approaches to treatment use including active, passive, and more autonomous approaches. Family obligations and transportation barriers posed challenges to accessing treatment. Lack of health insurance was a barrier affecting multiple aspects of recovery. Participants often desired shared decision making. Several types of perceived discrimination were discussed including race, gender, insurance, and weight. Facilitators were often related to positive communication or athletic program resources. CONCLUSION: Facilitators included shared decision making, provider empathy and encouragement, and athletic program resources. Barriers included a lack of listening to patients' concerns, lack of health insurance, transportation challenges, and perceived discrimination.

metadata.title: Fluoroscopy-Guided Intra-Articular Hip Corticosteroid Injections: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Utility, Technique, and Steroid Selection.
metadata.abstract: Intra-articular hip corticosteroid injection is a practical option for selected patients with hip pain, particularly osteoarthritis, and may also clarify whether symptoms arise from the hip rather than the lumbar spine or periarticular structures. This review evaluates the diagnostic and therapeutic utility of injections performed under fluoroscopy, summarizes technique, and discusses steroid selection and dosing. # Recent Findings Randomized trials and contemporary syntheses support clinically meaningful short-term improvement in pain and function after image-guided hip corticosteroid injection, although durability is variable and repeated-injection data remain limited. Fluoroscopy provides continuous visualization of osseous landmarks and contrast-confirmed intra-articular spread. Ultrasound avoids radiation and may be more convenient depending on physician comfort level and ultrasound skills. Safety discussions have emphasized transient systemic effects, uncertain associations with rapidly progressive osteoarthritis, and the timing of injection before arthroplasty. # Summary Fluoroscopy-guided injection remains a reliable, reproducible diagnostic and therapeutic tool when the pain generator is uncertain or short-term symptom control may facilitate rehabilitation, bridge care, or support shared surgical decision-making. Benefit depends on careful patient selection, technically confirmed intra-articular delivery, conservative dosing, and explicit counseling that relief is usually temporary and that structural disease is not reversed.

metadata.title: Is the annular ligament disrupted in Monteggia fracture-dislocations? A cadaveric mechanistic study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Monteggia fracture-dislocation is characterized by an ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation. The mechanisms of dislocation and annular ligament integrity remain unclear. This study established a cadaveric Monteggia fracture-dislocation model to investigate radial head dislocation and associated annular ligament injury. METHODS: Twelve upper limbs from 6 fresh-frozen cadavers (mean age at death, 83 years; 1 male, 5 females) were examined. Soft tissues were removed while preserving the bones, ligaments, capsules, forearm interosseous membrane, and biceps tendon insertions. The humeroulnar joint was fixed at 90° flexion, and the ulna was manually fractured to create a Bado type I (direct-blow) Monteggia fracture-dislocation model. The annular ligament, quadrate ligament, oblique cord (Weitbrecht ligament), and forearm interosseous membrane were evaluated. RESULTS: Ulnar fracture created forearm deformity, causing the radius to contact the triangular fulcrum. Continued manual loading caused the radius to pivot around the fulcrum. The annular ligament remained intact in 11 of 12 limbs; 1 specimen showed injury at the annular ligament-capsular junction. In 11 limbs, the radial head was dislocated beneath the distal margin of the annular ligament. One quadrate ligament rupture occurred; the oblique cord and forearm interosseous membrane remained intact. CONCLUSION: In this standardized cadaveric direct-blow model, anterior radial head dislocation occurred in 11 of 12 limbs, beneath the distal margin of an intact annular ligament. These findings demonstrate that annular ligament rupture is not required for radial head dislocation in the described experimental setting. This mechanism provides a possible anatomic explanation for difficult reduction in selected cases.

metadata.title: Associations between countermovement jump impulse and running kinetics following ACL reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: Persistent deficits in lower-limb loading are commonly observed following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may influence running biomechanics. Countermovement jump (CMJ) impulse can provide a phase-specific measure of force-time characteristics to reflect limb loading capacity; however, its relationship with running kinetics remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify phase-specific CMJ impulse following ACLR and examine associations with vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) metrics during treadmill running at the return-to-running phase. Forty-two participants performed three unilateral and bilateral CMJs on dual force plates and ran at 8 km/hr on an instrumented treadmill. Concentric, eccentric braking, and landing impulses were calculated. Running variables included weight acceptance rate, weight acceptance peak force, and maximum applied force. Inter-limb differences were assessed using Wilcoxon/paired t-tests. Impulse-vGRF relationships were analysed using Pearson/Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression. The ACLR limb exhibited significant deficits across all unilateral and bilateral CMJ phases, except for unilateral landing impulse. Deficits were greatest for unilateral concentric impulse (Δ1.3Ns·kg-0.67, d = 1.49, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force limb symmetry index (LSI) was explained by unilateral concentric impulse LSI (adjusted R2 = 0.25, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric impulse (adjusted R2 = 0.38, p < 0.001). Weight acceptance peak force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric and landing impulses (adjusted R2 = 0.37, p < 0.001). No meaningful relationships were observed for eccentric impulses or weight acceptance rate metrics. These findings indicate that jump impulse testing may provide clinically relevant indicators of running kinetics.

metadata.title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
metadata.abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

metadata.title: Test-Retest Reliability of Soft Tissue Vibration Variables Across an Outdoor 5-km Run.
metadata.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the test-retest reliability of soft tissue vibration (STV) measurements taken superficial to the medial gastrocnemius during a 5-km outdoor run. Twenty-eight trained athlete participants (female: n = 14 and male: n = 14) wore a triaxial inertial measurement unit mounted on the skin superficial to their medial gastrocnemius (500 Hz) and performed two 5-km outdoor runs on different days at a controlled, individualized pace. STV outcome measures-peak acceleration, damping coefficient, settling time, peak and median frequency, and power-were analyzed using a continuous wavelet transform from averaged running strides within the entire run and among three 1500-m segments from each testing session. Intraclass correlation coefficients reinforced good to excellent between-day reliability measures (.75-.92) for all STV outcome measures except peak frequency (.50) and moderate to excellent reliability when comparing days across the 3 segments of the run (.70-.94), except for peak frequency (.44-.57). No significant day × time interactions were observed (P = .06-.63). Overall, STV outcome measures assessed with an inertial measurement unit during outdoor running demonstrated good reliability, supporting methodologies to quantify STV in real-world settings with potential applications in running performance and injury prevention research.

metadata.title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
metadata.abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

metadata.abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

metadata.title: Aerobic exercise preconditioning enhances skeletal muscle resistance and recovery after contusion: involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Compared with passive recovery after injury, exercise preconditioning may provide an active strategy for improving the subsequent response of skeletal muscle to injury. This study aimed to investigate the effects of aerobic exercise preconditioning (AEP) on skeletal muscle injury (SMI) and post-injury repair, with particular focus on the involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and changes in PGC-1α acetylation. METHODS: This study initially investigated the effects of continuous aerobic exercise on skeletal muscle in healthy mice. Subsequently, the influence of AEP on injury severity and regenerative repair of the gastrocnemius muscle was examined in mice with SMI. Western blotting was used to determine the expression levels of SIRT1 and PGC-1α proteins, immunoprecipitation was performed to assess the acetylation status of PGC-1α, and qRT-PCR was used to analyze the expression of genes associated with mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers and muscle regeneration. Finally, the involvement of SIRT1 signaling in the AEP-associated response to SMI was further examined using the pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor EX527. RESULTS: Continuous aerobic exercise was associated with increased SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling and changes in mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers in the gastrocnemius muscle of healthy mice. AEP was associated with reduced injury-related changes and an improved post-injury repair profile in mice with SMI. During the early stage after injury, AEP was accompanied by sustained SIRT1/ PGC-1α signaling and reduced PGC-1α acetylation. Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 with EX527 partially attenuated the AEP-associated protective and reparative effects on the injured gastrocnemius muscle. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that AEP establishes an adaptive state in skeletal muscle that is associated with reduced injury-related damage and an enhanced post-injury reparative response. The SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and altered PGC-1α acetylation may contribute to these AEP-associated effects.

metadata.title: Relationships Between Isometric Belt Squat Force and Vertical Jump Performance Across Knee Joint Angles.
metadata.abstract: Rebelo, A, Ripley, N, Weakley, J, and Comfort, P. Relationships between isometric belt squat force and vertical jump performance across knee joint angles. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the relationships between vertical jump performance and isometric belt squat force assessed at 2 knee joint angles (120° and 90°) and to compare outcomes across age groups in male and female athletes. One hundred and twenty subjects (20.3 ± 6.5 years, 1.77 ± 0.12 m, 71.0 ± 13.3 kg) performed countermovement jumps, squat jumps, and isometric belt squat tests at 120° and 90° on dual force platforms. Between-group differences were analyzed using 1-way or Welch's analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc analyses. Associations were examined using Pearson's correlations with Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds (p < 0.002), while omnibus tests used corrected alpha levels where applicable. Isometric belt squat net peak force demonstrated weak-to-moderate associations with jump height across tasks (r = 0.36-0.55). Associations between net force at 200 milliseconds and jump height were moderate at 90° (r = 0.45-0.52), whereas net force at 100 milliseconds showed negligible associations to jump height. Older athletes produced significantly higher absolute isometric net peak force than younger groups only at 90° knee flexion (up to ∼860 N difference), with moderate-to-large effects (g = 0.67-0.80), whereas relative net peak force did not differ between age categories. These findings indicate that the isometric belt squat can be confidently used to monitor maximal lower-limb force capacity across knee angles, with the 90° position offering greater sensitivity for distinguishing strength levels between age groups.

metadata.title: Shallow under load? Prevalence of acetabular morphologies and their association with sport exposure during skeletal maturation in professional female football players: a retrospective study using data from the PROFE cohort.
metadata.abstract: We aimed to report the prevalence of acetabular morphologies in professional female footballers and explore the association between these morphologies and sport exposure during the period of skeletal maturation. 100 professional female footballers (200 hips) were included. Athletes with a history of systemic disease were excluded. Questionnaires obtained information on previous sport frequencies and age of menarche. Participants reported the minimum hours of sport played weekly during three age categories/stages of growth: cartilaginous hypertrophy (8-10 years), skeletal growth (11-12 years), and closure of growth plates (13-16 years). Participants underwent a pelvic radiograph. The Wiberg-center edge angle classified hips with normal coverage, borderline dysplasia, dysplasia or pincer morphology. Logistic regression models explored the association between prevalence of acetabular morphologies and minimum of sport hours played weekly in different age groups. Interactions with age of menarche were explored. From 200 hips, 32% were classified as having borderline dysplasia, 9% had dysplasia, 1% had pincer morphology, and 58% had normal coverage. Athletes with a later age of menarche had higher odds of dysplasia with increasing sport exposure between 8-10 (OR [95%CI] = 1.23 [1.05-1.44]). p = 0.011) and 11-12 years (OR [95%CI] = 1.21 [1.06-1.38], p = 0.006) compared to those with an earlier age of menarche. Skeletal maturation might be an important period for the development of acetabular morphology in female footballers. Exposure to high‑load sport activity during skeletal maturation and age of menarche may contribute to the development of hip dysplasia in these athletes.

metadata.title: When Athletes Ask About Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy.
metadata.abstract: Athletes exposed to repetitive head impacts (RHI) may seek clinical evaluation because of concerns about chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neuropathologically defined disease that cannot currently be diagnosed during life. As public awareness of CTE has expanded, clinicians face challenges communicating diagnostic uncertainty, interpreting non-specific symptoms, and addressing concerns about future neurological health. This Current Opinion examines the widening gap between public expectations and scientific capability and considers its implications for athlete-centered care. We discuss how clinicians can acknowledge uncertainty without dismissing patients' concerns, identify potentially treatable contributors to symptoms without prematurely attributing them to neurodegenerative disease, and use shared decision-making to guide individualized evaluation and management. We also consider how concerns about CTE may influence decisions about continued participation and return-to-sport among current athletes. Meeting these challenges requires coordinated interdisciplinary care, evidence-based communication, and clinical approaches that prioritize meaningful intervention even when diagnostic certainty remains unavailable.
